title: BYD teases first humanoid robot Xiao Di for early-August debut in dealerships
subtitle: The world's largest EV maker previewed its first humanoid — designed to greet customers and present cars — pushing China's automakers deeper into the robot race with Tesla and Figure.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: BYD, the world's largest maker of electric vehicles, posted a teaser on July 25 through the WeChat account of its Di Space Zhengzhou venue confirming that its first humanoid robot — named Xiao Di — will make its public debut in early August. Executive vice president Stella Li has previously said BYD wants every one of its stores staffed with robots that introduce and demonstrate vehicles to customers, and the teaser positions Xiao Di as that first sales-floor unit rather than a factory or household product.

The mechanism matters as much as the mascot. Deploying a humanoid into dealerships is a shortcut around the two hardest robotics problems — safety in open environments and business-model uncertainty — because a car showroom has controlled floor space, predictable customer interactions, and a captive audience willing to interact with a novelty. BYD sells cars through a large dealer network in China and abroad, so a demo-ready humanoid gives the company a distribution channel that pure-play robot startups still lack.

It also opens a second front in an accelerating field. Tesla is ramping Optimus Gen 3 in Fremont, Figure AI is shipping Figure 03 units into BMW's Spartanburg plant, UBTech's U1 companion robot took 13,000+ pre-orders, and Booster's T2 flagship platform launched earlier this month. Every one of these is a different bet on where humanoids earn their first commercial dollar — factory, warehouse, home, or retail. BYD is now placing its chip on retail.

For learners, the useful framing is this: robotics doesn't win by beating a benchmark, it wins by finding the environment where the current level of capability is already useful. A greeter robot in a controlled showroom does not need to fold laundry or navigate a curb. When you evaluate any embodied-AI claim, ask what environment it is designed for — that constraint tells you more about whether it will actually ship than the demo video does.
